items.label: A
items.critique: Breathless exclamations, '!?', 'lad', grand stakes ('All Nox is now in peril') and the slightly garbled 'At happier other times' are the campaign's own melodrama and rough edges.

items.label: B
items.critique: 'I surmise', '-- dead or alive', 'young sir' repeated, an exact gold sum and a bystander who walks in to take over the prisoner: Westwood's slightly stiff, formal bounty voice.

items.label: C
items.critique: Plain and short, close to Nox, but the invented trade detail ('basins', 'ore washer') is worldbuilding colour Westwood rarely spent on a side quest.

items.label: D
items.critique: 'Worse than the pox', a reward that is a title and free passage, 'I insist', and a journal naming the mechanic ('Charm and banish') are pure campaign.

items.label: E
items.critique: Flat, functional exposition ('Unfortunately, a foul little urchin has moved into the cave'), a named key colour, a petition as gate token, and the deadpan 'Excellent! You've killed the Urchin.'

items.label: F
items.critique: Packs a setup with alibi ('Mayor's men up at the north gate, nobody else can go') into one breath; the bow-needs-arrows quip is a writer's joke rather than Nox's plain thanks.

items.label: G
items.critique: 'Sorry, pal', 'Them Imps', 'cracking good', 'I owe you a big one' is a modern colloquial British register Nox's townsfolk never use.

items.label: H
items.critique: Starts mid-conversation ('Actually, business has been somewhat slow'), polite measured shopkeeper prose, ellipsis before '100 in gold!' and a plug for the shop: very Westwood.

items.label: I
items.critique: A comic goose rescue with the player asking for gold off-page ('Gold, you say? Lots of it?') is a knowing gag; the '?!' and the doubled 'she's safe!' read as imitation.

items.label: J
items.critique: Five pages stacking stakes, key, guide, potion and a follow-up hook is overloaded; 'out of the black depths' and 'You're a real hero!' are generic fantasy rather than Nox's plainness.

tells: Westwood's givers speak in a stiff, slightly formal register ('I surmise', 'somewhat slow of late', 'I insist') with occasional awkward phrasing; the new texts lean colloquial and modern ('pal', 'cracking good', 'I owe you a big one').
Westwood's rewards are concrete and stated plainly: an exact gold sum, a title, passage, a petition; the new texts make the reward a joke or a quip.
New texts over-justify the setup (why nobody else can go, how the monsters got in, which trade suffered) and pack several handouts into one offer.
Westwood's journal lines are short imperatives that may name the mechanic ('Charm and banish'); the new ones are longer and stack places and owners into one line or two sentences.
Westwood's humour is deadpan and incidental; the new texts stage comic set-pieces (a goose, a stolen hat, a bow without arrows).
